cells.tense: You are reading what this inheritance is actually doing, with your hand on it.
cells.ask: Name one inherited practice you've stopped repeating because it no longer fits, and one you've chosen to keep.
cells.core:
You can step back far enough to see what's being handed down, and close enough that it's still yours to work in. Most people get one half or the other — devotion that can't see itself, or distance that costs them the room.

What you see keeps opening instead of closing. You can say what your people are doing and mean it, and revise it later, because the picture isn't finished and you don't need it to be. So what you pass on stays answerable, and people can carry it without you standing over them. That's the version that keeps the thing alive.
cells.sheetLine: You know what you inherited without sealing it shut.
cells.place: inside a shared inheritance — the customs, language and practices handed down and still in use

cells.tense: You are already measuring who is getting it right and who is falling short of it.
cells.ask: Catch one moment where you rank someone against how it's supposed to be done, and say what they're doing right, nothing added.
cells.core:
You can see the whole shape of what's being handed down, and lately you're using it as a standard. You know how the thing should be done and you're keeping score — who's carrying it right, who's diluting it, who hasn't earned a say. The verdict runs ahead of you and lands before you've looked at the person in front of you.

Being right about the shape doesn't require anyone to fail it. Correction is a direction, not a sentence: pick one thing worth carrying forward and put your weight there, instead of against whoever's holding it badly. That's a different kind of work, and it leaves the young ones somewhere to stand.
cells.sheetLine: You can see what's right, and now you're grading people by it.
cells.place: inside a shared inheritance — the customs, language and practices handed down and still in use

cells.tense: You were standing outside it, watching how it was done, and you never quite took a place in it.
cells.ask: Show up to one thing your people do regularly and stay until it ends, without deciding on the way home whether it meant anything.
cells.core:
Holding it well looks like taking part and being changed by it — doing the thing at the usual time with the usual people, and letting it be yours. You've been close to that. From outside you can describe exactly what they do and why, and the description has replaced standing in the room, so nothing reaches you as yours. That can feel like keeping an open mind. Mostly it's the door staying shut and your weight off it.

What brings you back isn't a bigger insight about the whole thing. It's smaller: one gathering, one inherited habit done plainly, no verdict required. Practice reaches further than analysis here.
cells.sheetLine: You can describe it perfectly and still not take part.

cells.tense: You are already reading how this group works, and you talk about it as though you weren't.
cells.ask: Say one true thing you've noticed about how your people's customs actually work, to someone who's been in it longer.
cells.core:
You notice how your people's customs hold together — which parts are load-bearing, which ones are followed without belief, which ones survive only because nobody's looked at them. That's working knowledge. And you keep folding it into sentences about how the thing just is, as though anyone standing where you stand would see the same.

Calling it yours doesn't crown you. It makes you answerable, which is a lighter load than carrying a mismatched one. The people who built the customs probably want them looked at by someone with eyes. Say it out loud and let somebody hear it and disagree.
cells.sheetLine: You already see how it works, and you call that just how it works.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person reads the wider pattern before others do or has stood at the edge of a tradition and left — the record shows the capacity, not the biography. A reader could say this is happening in a family or a workplace instead of anything they'd call a tradition, and the ask still works there, since saying which parts you actually keep and which you're only carrying can be done in any room. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'you were already outside it' — it flatters the reader's vantage instead of describing the work, so it's out. Same with anything that tells them what they concluded back then; the cells stay on what the capacity is doing now and let the person supply the rest.
